Aerial Wildlife 
Survey Report 
2016 Willmore Mountain Goat Surveys 
 
Background 
Annual minimum total count (MTC) surveys for mountain goats have been conducted in the Willmore Wilderness 
Park and adjacent areas since 1974. The goal of these annual surveys is to collect data on population trends, 
distribution and herd composition, and to monitor the status of these mountain goat herds. It is particularly 
important to assess the status of the population and management risk associated with the allocation of hunting 
licences within mountain complexes that have a sufficient population to sustain harvest. Only three complexes, Mt 
Deveber (6), Llama-Turret (5) and North Persimmon (9; Figure 1), have had a large enough population of goats 
for a sustainable hunt in the past few years (example: more than 50 goats observed). The objectives of this 
survey were to assess the status of mountain goat populations in the three hunted complexes. An addition al 
complex, Monoghan, was also assessed to inform general population trends. 
 
Survey method 
A Bell 206B helicopter was flown counter-clockwise around each mountain complex between timberline and ridge 
top. Air speed ranged from 120 to 150 km/hr. The left front passenger was responsible for navigating, observing 
and plotting. Global Positioning System (GPS) locations  were recorded for each group of goats. The rear 
passengers were responsible for observing and  recording species classification and numbers onto field data 
sheets. All flights were conducted in the early morning and in the evening during the goats’ most active periods 
and when winds were typically minimal. 
  
We compared annual total counts of non-kids (adult and yearling mountain goats) for each complex to the long-
term average for each of the four complexes. To assess trends in productivity, we pooled classified animals 
across complexes. We used a global population index to assess trends in abundance through time at the regional 
scale (example: Willmore Wilderness Park): A value of 1 represents average mountain goat abundance, 0.5 and 
2.0 represent half and double the average mountain goat abundance for the region respectively. The index was 
calculated by dividing the total number of non-kids observed in a given year by the sum of the long term averages 
for each complex flown in that year. 
Results 
Surveys were completed in Mt. Deveber, Llama-Turret, North Persimmon, and Monoghan complexes from June 
27 to 28, 2016, for a total survey effort of 14.0 hours of flight time. Weather and survey conditions were ideal for 
Mt. Deveber, Llama-Turret and North Persimmon with clear skies and calm winds. In contrast, weather conditions 
during the survey of the Monoghan complex deteriorated midway and visibility was compromis ed by heavy rain 
and low light conditions for the last ¼ of the survey. A total of 176 mountain goats were observed from 33

independent groups across all completed complexes. Of this total, 131 adults, 8 yearlings and  37 kids were 
observed (Table 1). The kid: non-kid ratio was 0.28. 
  
With the exception of Mt. Deveber, the population levels observed for adult and yearling mountain goats were 
lower than the long term averages for each surveyed complex (Figure 2). When pooled, the kid/non -kid ratio was 
equivalent to the long term average for all four complexes combined (Figure 3).  
 
Discussion 
The total number of adults and yearlings observed in each complex (with the exception of Mt. Deveber) are lower 
than the long term averages. Productivity was high in 2016 likely as a result of the extremely mild winter in 
2015/2016.   Currently, total goat counts for Mt. Deveber are above 50, while total counts for Llama -turret and 
North Persimmon are just below 50 (N=46 and 45, respectively). While the total count of goats observed on the 
Monoghan complex decreased from 48 in 2015 to 11 in 2016, this decrease may at least partly reflect the 
movement of individuals between Monoghan and Rockslide complexes. The Rockslide complex was impacted by 
a major fire in the summer of 2015 when the goat surveys were conducted and goats were observed displaced to 
the border of the two complexes, likely inflating the 2015 Monoghan population estimate. Weather conditions 
deteriorated during the survey of the Monaghan complex and budget constraints did not permit us to resurvey the 
complex. While we provide the results of this survey for information they should be interpreted judiciously in this 
context.  Overall, mountain goat populations within the Willmore continue to exhibit either declines  or depressed 
populations (the exception being the Mt Deveber complex).
